web.title: Dangerous and Reckless Message of Using Extrajudicial Killings as a Shield for Failure to Maintain Law and Order;  TIB Calls for Withdrawal of IGPâs Remarks and Accountability
web.description: Press Release Dhaka, 26 October 2026: Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB) has strongly condemned and expressed deep concern over the Inspector General of Policeâs (IGP) remarks that the police would resort to crossfire, if necessary, to maintain law and order, provided the government gives its approval. According to TIB, the remarks send a dangerous message by presenting extrajudicial killings as an acceptable means of crime control, rather than addressing failures in maintaining law and order and institutional weaknesses. Describing the remarks as an expression of utter disregard for the Constitution and the rule of law, TIB has demanded their immediate withdrawal, accountability of the IGP, and accountability for making a declaration that contradicts the governmentâs stated position against extrajudicial killings. ... TIB Executive Director Dr. Iftekharuzzaman said, âIs the police chief seeking to use the discredited practice of crossfire as a shield for the policeâs failure to maintain law and order? Does seeking to legitimise extrajudicial killings by making them conditional on government approval amount to an admission of failure to combat crime through lawful means? The responsibility of the police is to conduct professional investigations, identify offenders and bring the accused to trial on the basis of admissible evidence. Presenting crossfire as an alternative cannot resolve institutional weaknesses; rather, it is an example of professional bankruptcy. In the same remarks, the IGP spoke of discharging duties in accordance with the law and the Constitution, while also saying that the police would resort to crossfire if the government approved it. These two positions are contradictory. No government approval can legitimise an extrajudicial killing. web.title: Govt steps up anti-corruption drive with disciplinary action, 23 directives - The Bangladesh Today
web.description: Govt steps up anti-corruption drive with disciplinary action, 23 directives - The Bangladesh Today Published : October 26, 2026 # Govt steps up anti-corruption drive with disciplinary action, 23 directives The government has escalated its drive against institutional corruption and financial irregularities, rolling out a series of high-profile disciplinary actions, digitisation initiatives, and stringent administrative directives. Rooted in the "Bangladesh First" guiding philosophy, the current administration is executing a comprehensive strategy to establish transparency, enforce institutional discipline, and curb the misuse of public funds across vital sectors. Underscoring this zero-tolerance policy, the Security Services Division of the Home Ministry recently issued separate gazette notifications enforcing severe punitive measures against senior officials under the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 2018. Former Panchagarh District Jail jailer Md Abdul Fattah was formally dismissed from service following a departmental inquiry that unearthed the embezzlement of Tk 1.33 crore in prison food-supply funds through fraudulent ration bills. In a separate case, Department of Narcotics Control Chief Chemical Examiner Dr Dulal Krishna Saha was sent into compulsory retirement after an inquiry proved he defrauded the state of Tk 3.15 lakh by submitting forged court summonses to claim illicit travel allowances for unattended hearings. Beyond these individual cases, the crackdown is backed by 23 strict administrative directives issued by the Cabinet Division, following a high-level conclave of 61 secretaries, with criminal proceedings simultaneously being pursued under the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) Act, 2004 and the Penal Code. Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed declared that the government is aggressively dismantling the systemic vulnerabilities that breed corruption by enforcing total transparency and delivering swift, hassle-free public services. He revealed that a formidable anti-graft infrastructure is already in motion, anchored by 495 localized corruption-prevention committees across cities, districts, and upazilas, alongside intensified crackdowns by the Anti-Corruption Commission's (ACC) intelligence and enforcement divisions. Pointing to the rapid deployment of national hotlines 999, 333, and 106 to weaponize public whistleblowing, Ahmed issued a stern warning that the state is actively leveraging the full force of existing laws to prosecute corruption, financial irregularities, institutional waste, and any abuse of official power. To systematically dismantle deep-seated bureaucratic corruption and eliminate exploitative middlemen, the government is pioneering aggressive digitisation and oversight frameworks across three key areas: health and education. In the land sector, cashless transactions have been heavily institutionalised through an online land development tax system alongside drone-based digital land surveys, digital access to historical records, the Tejgaon Citizen Service Centre, and a 24-hour grievance hotline (16122). In healthcare, reform measures include the complete digitisation of medical service logs, hospital monitoring committees, rigorous tracking of the pharmaceutical supply chain, and regular law enforcement drives to evict brokers from public hospitals. Concurrently, the Ministry of Education has launched a multi-phase white paper investigating financial anomalies and management weaknesses spanning nearly two decades from fiscal year 2008-09 to 2024-25. To eradicate nepotism, all future teacher appointments will transition to independent, centralized commission examinations, while administrative processes like Monthly Pay Order (MPO) enlistments, institutional transfers, and promotions are being fully automated alongside the digital publication of institutional budgets and student stipends. To sustain this institutional overhaul, the ACC has deployed targeted intelligence units and established 495 localized corruption-prevention committees spanning cities, districts, and upazilas, while public complaints are being funnelled directly into national emergency hotlines including 999, 333, and 106. Project monitoring has also been reinforced across multiple tiers, including Project Implementation Committees and the Implementation Monitoring and Evaluation Division, alongside newly mobilized three-member monitoring teams led by Additional Secretaries to conduct independent oversight. Experts emphasize that the ultimate challenge lies in translating these regulatory frameworks into lasting institutional culture through consistent enforcement, watertight procurement controls, and absolute independence for state oversight bodies. Analysts conclude that impartial, evidence-based investigations that strictly respect due process will be the true benchmark of success, holding the genuine potential to restore public trust, eliminate systemic harassment, and deliver transparent, efficient, and accountable public service delivery across the nation. web.title: Upholding Human Rights & Public Safety: How Far Is ...
web.description: Upholding Human Rights & Public Safety: How Far Is Bangladesh? â Global Issues # Upholding Human Rights & Public Safety: How Far Is Bangladesh? * Opinion by Shahiduzzaman (dhaka, bangladesh) * Monday, October 26, 2026 * Inter Press Service DHAKA, Bangladesh, October 26 (IPS) - Bangladesh has achieved remarkable economic progress over the past few decades. Its garment industry has become globally important, millions of people have entered the workforce, and private businesses have expanded across manufacturing, services, technology and trade. But economic growth alone does not create a healthy business environment. Businesses also need predictable laws, safe workplaces, fair competition, protection of property and contracts, and respect for the rights of workers, consumers and communities. Shahiduzzaman The important question is therefore not simply whether Bangladesh is open for business. It is whether Bangladesh can create an environment where economic growth and human rights, investment and public safety, and business success and accountability go together. There has been progress, but significant gaps remain. The World Bankâs Enterprise Surveys have repeatedly identified corruption, infrastructure, access to finance and regulatory obstacles among the challenges faced by businesses in Bangladesh. These problems increase the cost and uncertainty of doing business, particularly for smaller enterprises. The World Bank has also emphasised that effective regulations and institutions governing business registration, licensing, inspections and property rights are essential for reducing business risks while protecting consumers, public health and safety. Corruption is particularly damaging because it creates an uneven playing field. When businesses believe that personal connections or unofficial payments are necessary to obtain services, licences or approvals, honest businesses can be placed at a disadvantage. It also weakens confidence in government institutions and discourages investment. The problem is not necessarily a lack of laws. Bangladesh has numerous laws and regulatory agencies. The deeper problem is often implementation and enforcement. Rules that are reasonable on paper have little value if they are applied selectively, slowly or inconsistently. This gap is also visible in the rule of law. The World Justice Projectâs 2025 Rule of Law Index ranked Bangladesh 125th among 143 countries, although Bangladeshâs overall score improved by 1.3 per cent from the previous year. The index examines areas including fundamental rights, regulatory enforcement, civil justice, criminal justice and order and security. Human rights and workplace safety are another critical part of responsible business. Bangladesh has made important progress since the Rana Plaza disaster, particularly in the garment sector. More recently, the country took a significant step by ratifying ILO Conventions 155 and 187 on occupational safety and health and Convention 190 on violence and harassment at work in November 2025. The ILO described these ratifications as an important commitment to safer workplaces and workersâ rights. However, ratification is not the same as implementation. The ILO itself makes clear that ratification represents a commitment to progressively align national laws and practices with international standards; it does not mean that full compliance automatically exists on the day of ratification. The real challenge is therefore to ensure that workplace safety rules are consistently enforced, labour inspectors have adequate resources and independence, and workers can report violations without fear of retaliation. Public safety and institutional trust are equally important. A business environment cannot be stable when citizens lack confidence in the institutions responsible for law enforcement and justice. The Asia Foundationâs 2024 survey of 6,510 Bangladeshis found that only 20.5 per cent considered the police to have very high integrity. Trust in the judiciary was 38.2 per cent. The survey also showed that trust in both institutions had declined from 2022 levels. Other countries demonstrate that stronger institutions and economic development can advance together. Singapore provides one example of the importance of consistent enforcement and institutional integrity. According to Transparency Internationalâs 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index, Singapore scored 84 out of 100 and ranked third among 182 countries. The index measures perceptions of public-sector corruption, based on expert assessments and business surveys. Vietnam provides another useful comparison because, like Bangladesh, it has built a strong export-oriented manufacturing economy. The World Bank says Vietnamâs economic success over recent decades has been strongly supported by export-oriented foreign investment, but argues that further growth requires regulatory reform and higher productivity. Vietnam has introduced a programme to simplify or reduce business regulations and, by December 2023, had simplified or reduced 2,789 regulations. Its National Public Services Portal had also digitised more than 70 per cent of public administrative services. So, what should Bangladesh do? First, the government must close the gap between laws and enforcement. Regulations should be clear, simple and applied equally. Second, government services such as licences, permits, taxation, customs and inspections should increasingly be digitised. Clear deadlines, published fees and traceable decisions can reduce opportunities for unofficial payments. Third, regulatory agencies must be more accountable. Complaints against officials should be independently investigated, and disciplinary measures should follow transparent procedures. Fourth, labour inspection must be strengthened. Workplace safety should not become a priority only after accidents occur. Employers who violate safety standards should face meaningful consequences, while compliant businesses should not be placed at a competitive disadvantage. Fifth, police and justice institutions need to rebuild public confidence through professional training, independent complaint mechanisms, timely investigations and equal application of the law. Finally, businesses, workers, civil society and consumers should have meaningful opportunities to participate in regulatory reform. Policies imposed without consultation often fail to address problems experienced on the ground. Bangladesh does not have to choose between business growth and human rights. In fact, sustainable economic growth increasingly depends on both. Safe workers are more productive, predictable regulations encourage investment, fair competition rewards innovation, and trusted institutions reduce the risks and costs of doing business. The ultimate test is simple: Can an entrepreneur compete without connections? Can a worker work without fear? Can a consumer obtain justice? Can a business receive government services without unofficial payments? And can every citizen expect the law to be applied fairly? If Bangladesh can answer these questions through effective institutions rather than promises, it can build a business environment based not only on economic opportunity, but also on human rights, public safety, fairness and public trust. ***Shahiduzzaman** is the Editor and CEO of News Network. shahiduzzaman@newsnetwork-bd.org* ***This story was originally published by The Financial Express***
